story.logline: The Stillness has frozen every gate in cell V-7. Restart each one by its true rule before the cell's gradients drain away.
story.objective: Restart the gates and wake the nucleus

restoredLine.text: The pore's turning! Every conduit you lit is pouring into it.

approach.text: The Stillness froze this stretch of membrane solid. Three specimen pods here, and one of them holds a Mimic.

instruction.text: Push the probe into the membrane and watch it. Then quarantine the pod whose claim the membrane disproves.

tutorial.text: Your depth dial drives the needle. My readouts track how polar the membrane is at its tip, and what that costs an ion.

insight.text: Healthy membrane parts around the needle and closes behind it. Only the frozen ridge stays stiff.

hints.text: Forget the textbook diagram. Watch what the heads do while the needle goes in; that's what this ground is made of.
Lipids with oily tails make a layer that flows around the probe and closes behind it. That's no wall.
The Mimic's claim: "The membrane is a rigid wall with fixed holes in it."

default.text: That pod's claim held up against the real membrane. Push again, and watch which claim the heads keep breaking.

success.text: A membrane is not a wall. It's a film that flows, and only proteins give it doors.

payoffLine.text: Mimic quarantined! And look at the ridge. It's melting back into a path.

approach.text: Watch the small ones. Small doesn't mean welcome.

instruction.text: Route each molecule: straight through the bilayer on the Oil Road, or through the Crossing Gate's ring.

tutorial.text: Pick a molecule, then a lane. It queues where you send it; nothing crosses until the whole cargo is routed.

insight.text: The oily core between the heads is the real border. Size gets a molecule noticed; chemistry gets it through.

hints.text: Size is a clue, not the rule. Pip's water lens is on now: see which molecules drag a shell of water with them.
Check whether each one is polar or charged. The oily core between the heads turns away anything with a charge.
Na+ is smaller than O2 and still can't cross alone. Charge beats size, every time.

default.text: The road refused one. Check its charge and polarity before its size, then reroute it.

line.text: Size fooled you there. Even the smallest ion on this yard bounces off the oil.
Size isn't what the heads check. An oily visitor slips through them whatever its size.

success.text: Oil lets the oily through. Charged and polar visitors need a protein door, however small they are.

payoffLine.text: Every molecule took the right road! The Crossing Gate is spinning up.

approach.text: The Balance Lock only opens when both sides of this tank are even. Right now the dye is piled on the left.

instruction.text: Set the dye load and watch the tank. Then quarantine the pod whose story about the dye is a lie.

tutorial.text: The dye dial refills the left chamber. On my top readout the white dot is the left side now, the green dot the right.

insight.text: Watch the ringed tracer. It wanders, doubles back, and never once checks where the crowd is.

hints.text: Follow the tracer, the one with the white ring. Watch whether it ever seems to know where the crowd is.
Each particle wanders at random. More start on the crowded side, so more happen to cross from there.
The Mimic's claim: "The dye particles head for the empty side on purpose."

default.text: That pod's story matched the tank. Watch the tracer's trail for a while before you choose again.

success.text: No particle has a plan. Diffusion is just what a crowd of random steps adds up to.

payoffLine.text: Mimic quarantined. The tank's evening out, and the Balance Lock is levelling off.

approach.text: A test cell in a salt bath, and a raft stuck in a dry lock. It won't float until something crosses that window.

instruction.text: Salt the bath and watch the test cell. Then quarantine the pod whose story about what moves doesn't hold.

tutorial.text: The salt dial sets the bath. Below two percent the pods go quiet: their claims are about a salty bath.

insight.text: Those salt cubes have been bouncing off the cell all morning. The membrane is fussy about what it lets in.

hints.text: Two things could cross: the water or the dissolved salt. Only one of them gets through a bilayer.
Osmosis is water moving toward the side with more solute. Watch where the blue droplets go.
The Mimic's claim: "Salt rushes into the cell until both sides match."

default.text: That pod was honest. Crank the salt up and down, and watch what the white salt cubes actually do.

success.text: Salt stays where it is. Water goes where the solute is, and it'll lift a raft to get there.

payoffLine.text: Quarantined! Now I'm salting the raft lock. Water will follow the salt in and float you up. Step aboard!

approach.text: Mm. Visitors. I am Poro. Water passes through my waist in single file, and nothing else. Now, the sluices.
Cells are drifting down the sluice canal. Each lock needs a label before its cell passes. Quick hands, Diver.

instruction.text: Label each lock's bath before its cell drifts past: hypotonic, isotonic, or hypertonic.

tutorial.text: Each cell gives you eight seconds at the Label Lock. One that drifts past unlabelled spins into the Eddy and counts as a miss.

insight.text: Poro's basins have sorted cells for a billion years. Swell, shrink, or hold steady: the bath decides which.

hints.text: The label describes the bath around the cell, not the cell itself.
Hyper means more solute outside, so water leaves. Hypo means less solute outside, so water comes in.
A swelling cell means water came in, so its bath had less solute than the cell.

default.text: One lock's label doesn't fit its bath. Compare the dots inside that cell with the dots around it.

line.text: Hyper means more solute, not more water. A bath that's nearly all water is the one with the fewest dots.

success.text: Tonicity always compares the bath with the cell. Hyper outside, water leaves. Hypo outside, water arrives.

payoffLine.text: The sluice is draining! Steps are coming up out of the water, and that's our way up.

after.text: Mm. Well sorted. The water will remember you. Take my ledger; it is heavy with droplets.

approach.text: The Pump Hall doors. More cargo waiting, and two gates: the Glide Gate, and the Pump Gate that burns ATP.

instruction.text: Route each cargo: passive, down its slope for free, or active, uphill through the pump at a cost.

tutorial.text: Each cargo floats over its own ramp; the dense end is the crowded side. My ATP readout shows what the Pump Gate would spend.

insight.text: Plenty of proteins in this yard, and most of them never touch a spark of ATP.

hints.text: Ignore whether a protein is involved. Look at the slope under each cargo, and which way it has to go.
Downhill is always passive, protein or not. A carrier is a door, not an engine.
Only the cargo heading toward the more crowded side costs ATP.

default.text: One cargo went to a gate that won't take it. Check its slope: rolling down on its own, or being pushed up.

line.text: A protein on the route doesn't mean a fuel bill. Downhill cargo rides a door for free.

success.text: A protein can open a door without paying a thing. Energy is only spent when the cargo climbs.

payoffLine.text: Threshold open! The Carrier Door is turning. Everybody into the pocket!

approach.text: Two tanks, one high and one low, and a pump between them. Three pods argue about what that pump does.

instruction.text: Feed the pump ATP and watch the tanks. Then quarantine the pod that has pumps backwards.

tutorial.text: The ATP dial feeds the pump. On my readouts white is the high tank, green the low one, and gold is what you're spending.

insight.text: At zero feed the gap between those tanks bleeds away down the leak trough. That's the Stillness in miniature.

hints.text: A cell spends ATP on moving things for a reason. Try the feed at zero and watch the tanks.
If everything only ran downhill, nobody would ever need to pay for it.
The Mimic's claim: "Transport always runs down the gradient, so pumps just speed it up."

default.text: That pod told the truth. Take the feed to zero, then up again, and watch which way the gap between the tanks goes.

success.text: A pump is a climber. It carries cargo uphill, from low to high, and ATP pays for every step.

payoffLine.text: Quarantined, and the lanterns are catching! The gantry has power. Up you go.

approach.text: There it is: the sodium-potassium pump. Biggest machine on this membrane, and someone pulled its cables.

instruction.text: Rewire the pump: link each socket to its value cartridge. Step the stage dial to test a cycle.

tutorial.text: Each cartridge loads exactly what its label says. Step the stage dial and the drum runs a cycle on what you loaded.

insight.text: Every beat of a nerve starts with this machine. The charge ledger shows what one cycle leaves behind.

hints.text: The counts aren't equal. That lopsidedness is the whole point of this machine.
More positive charge leaves than comes in each cycle. Count which ion leaves, and how many.
Three sodium out, two potassium in, one ATP.

default.text: The pump jammed at one stage. Find the socket whose cable won't hold and rethink that link.

line.text: Two out and two in moves no charge at all. The ledger needle never leaned; a balanced pump builds nothing.

success.text: Three out and two in leaves the inside a little negative. That lopsided pump is why nerves can fire.

payoffLine.text: It's cycling! Three out, two in, one spark of ATP, again and again. The Hall Gate is lifting.

approach.text: Four cells coming down the Return Sluice, and our barge is sitting on the mud.

instruction.text: For each lock, set the water flow before the cell drifts past: in, out, or no net movement.

tutorial.text: Same Label Lock, new valves. Hover one and ghost arrows show the flow it claims. Eight seconds per cell.

insight.text: Solute dots never leave their side of a membrane. Only the water gets to travel.

hints.text: Compare the solute dots inside and outside each cell.
Water goes toward the side with more solute.
Equal solute on both sides means no net movement at all.

default.text: One flow call was off. The salt doesn't move, so ask which side the water is heading toward.

line.text: Salt never makes the trip across. Watch the dots stay put, and let the water do the travelling.

success.text: You never have to watch the salt. Find where the solute is crowded, and the water's already on its way.

payoffLine.text: Every call right. The locks are filling, and the barge is rising to the Endocytosis Pit.

approach.text: No channel in this cell is big enough for the Halcyon. So the membrane is going to swallow us. On purpose.

instruction.text: Set the four stage plates in the order that brings us into the cell. One plate doesn't belong.

tutorial.text: The playback dial runs the membrane through your plates, slot by slot. Scrub it and watch the pit try each step.

insight.text: Nothing this big fits through a protein. The membrane will have to do the carrying itself, and that costs ATP.

hints.text: Something too big for any protein channel has to be wrapped up.
The membrane does the wrapping first, then closes the pocket.
Start at the moment of contact and end with the vesicle moving.

default.text: The Lift stalled partway. Scrub through your plates and find the step that can't happen yet.

line.text: Hold. The membrane cannot do that yet.
Nothing this size dissolves through us. The membrane must carry it, and carrying costs.

success.text: Big cargo can't pass through a door, so the membrane becomes the door. Folding and pinching both cost ATP.

payoffLine.text: We're folding in... pinching off... and we're in! Welcome to the cytoplasm, Diver.

instruction.text: Sort every cargo into a maw: simple diffusion, facilitated diffusion, or active transport.

tutorial.text: Cargo comes in three batches. Each maw opens as you pick it, and my ATP readout shows the Pump Maw's bill.

insight.text: Every crossing in this cell comes down to two things: which way the cargo is headed, and whether it dissolves in oil.

hints.text: Check two things per cargo: which way it's headed on its gradient, and whether it can dissolve through lipid alone.
Uphill is always active. Downhill with a protein is facilitated.
Only small nonpolar molecules cross alone.

default.text: One came back up. Take it from the top: the way it's headed first, then whether oil lets it through.

success.text: Oil for the small and nonpolar, a protein door for the rest, and ATP only for the climb. That's every crossing.

line.text: Hrrm. Two cargo to start. Show me you can tell a slope from a shove.
Two more. My pump maw is hungry, and it hates waste.
The last three. A billion years of pumping rides on these.

fail.text: Hrrm. That one came back up. Direction first. Then ask whether it can pass through oil.
Hrrm. My maws do not argue. They spit. Look at the slope under what I spat.

line.text: A door is not an engine. My pump maw will not pay for a downhill trip.
Downhill only, you think. Then nothing would ever climb, and my pump maw has climbed for a billion years.
Small is not welcome. Charge sinks in my oil maw like a stone.

plaques.title: The Two Faces
plaques.text: Each lipid has a head that loves water and two tails that flee it. Tails hide inside; heads face out.

plaques.title: Why Oil Says No
plaques.text: A charge wants water around it. The bilayer's oily core has none, so ions are turned away.

lines.text: Cell V-7, deep in living tissue. Its gates have gone still, and its gradients are draining away.
Hull's holding at seven nanometres, all hands dry. Welcome to the outside of a living cell, Diver.
Shrink complete. That wall ahead is the membrane. Nothing gets through it without a reason.
Bad news first: the Stillness hit this cell. Pumps stopped, gates locked, gradients flattening out.
When inside matches outside, a cell goes quiet for good. Equilibrium sounds calm. For a cell, it's the end.
Good news: every gate here is a machine, and machines restart. Set each one to its true rule and it runs.
What crosses, how, and at what cost. Get those right at every gate and we reach the nucleus.
I'll hold the Halcyon's helm. Pip goes with you. Pip, say hello. ...Pip says hello.
Gradient Meter reads twelve percent. Let's make it a hundred. Pip will blink at anything worth a closer look.
I have pumped for a billion years. Show me you know what costs energy.
Three maws. Oil, Channel, Pump. Feed each cargo to the right one. Waste my ATP and the vault stays shut.
The pore turns. Go. And tell the nucleus the pumps are running again.
The nucleus! You got the whole crew through by knowing what crosses, how, and at what cost.
Gradient Meter: one hundred percent. Inside and outside are different again. That difference is what alive means.
Oxygen through the oil, glucose on a carrier, water through Poro, sodium uphill for ATP. You rebuilt a cell's rules.
Bring Pip home, Diver. And, er... the cell next door is looking a little still, too.
